topics.title: What kind of solution is this?
topics.text:
Source: https://www.mathcounts.org/resources/problem-of-the-week/national-competition-3

2016 National MATHCOUNTS Team #8: The display on a calculator is broken so that when the calculator shows a number in decimal form, the tenths and hundredths digits of the number are never visible. Shawna enters a positive number N in the calculator and presses a button that gives the reciprocal of the integer in decimal form. The nine digits following the missing digits in the display are all threes. What is the sum of all the possible values of N?

MATHCOUNTS SolutionThe smallest value of N for which this would occur is 3, since we know the reciprocal of 3 is 1/3 and displays on the calculator as 0.33333333333. The largest value of N for which this could occur is 300, the reciprocal would display on the calculator as 0.00333333333. So we need to look for the other values are between 3 and 300 will also display 3s in the last nine digits on the screen. The repeating 3s in the reciprocal also occur for N = 12, 30 and 75. The sum of all the possible values of N is 3 +12 +30 + 75 + 300 = 420.


My solutionSince it ends in nine 3's, the reciprocal of N must be in the form X/100+1/300=(3X+1)/300, so the reciprocal of the reciprocal of N, N, is 300/(3X+1). This means 3X+1 is a factor of 300 because N is an integer.  The factors of 300 are {1,2,3,4,5,6,10,12,15,20,25,30,50,60,75,100,150,300}. The only possible values of 3X+1 are 1, 4, 10, 25, and 100, so N can be 3, 12, 30, 75 and 300. The sum of all the possible values of N is 3 +12 +30 + 75 + 300 = 420.

topics.title: 1997 AJHSME Problem 2
topics.text:
On the second problem of the 1997 AJHSME, it goes like this:



Ahn chooses a two-digit integer, subtracts it from 200, and doubles the result. What is the largest number Ahn can get?



http://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php?title=1997_AJHSME_Problems/Problem_2



It says that the correct answer is 380, which is what I got, out of all the choices. But theoretically, wouldn't you be able to use $-99$ as the two-digit integer?



Since it's an integer, it can be negative. You can subtract $-99$ from $200$, which is basically like adding 99 to 200. This gives you 299, and doubling that gives you 598. So wouldn't that be the correct answer?

Hmm... what should I do?

I will create a contest!

The test will contain 15 questions. The time limit is 30 minutes. No calculators allowed.

First three questions are 2 points each, next three are 3 points each, next three are 4 points each, next three are 5 points each, the last three are 6 points each. So there is a total of 60 points

Full rules will be posted later.

I will post sample questions later.

You may signup for test creator (3-5 people who create the questions), test solver (4-6 people who solve the questions and find any mathematical flaws or problems with the questions) reviewer(2-4 people who look for any problems in wording), or competitor (up to 60 people)

The test will be most probably be released early to mid-July and due 2-3 weeks after the release date.

Sample 2-Point question (Questions 1-3)There are ten people in a room; all have integer ages. Their ages form an arithmetic sequence. 9 of the 10 people's ages are prime numbers.  The same ten people meet two years later. How many people have prime ages on the second time they meet


Sample 5-Point Question (Questions 10-12)I drew a circle with a diameter of 7 inches. Then I drew a triangle that circumscribes the circle such that it has the smallest area possible. Then I cut out the triangle  and made it a dart board. I colored the circle red and then colored the rest of the dartboard blue. The red area is worth 100 points and the blue area is worth 50 points. I threw darts until I got at least 1000 points. Given that I will randomly throw the dart anywhere within 3 inches of the board, what is the most likely number of throws I will do?
